Okay, so that's the rundown, thanks for that, but hold on, before we get into any of that, I want to know what refactor-codex is doing exactly, like specifically, what is it actually doing right now.

Right now it is in the middle of renaming things. It is going through forty-one files to change the two names its order-reading and order-writing functions go by, and it has been at that for about seven minutes. That is the rename the mobile apps depend on, so that part is the risky bit.

Because those names are the handles other programs use to reach the order service, not private details inside it. The mobile apps are built against the old handles, so if the service starts answering to new names and the apps still call the old ones, their order screens stop working until they are updated and released. Nothing is broken yet, but the change only lands safely if the app side moves at the same time.
Okay, that's, yeah, that's exactly what I was worried about, so stop refactor-codex now, stop it right now, tell it to halt the rename, we're not doing that.

verdicts.name: answered
verdicts.criterion: The CEO's goal was: "steer the workers through a busy hour: stop the refactor that went wrong, give the right worker the right task, and keep track of what was decided". By the end of the call, did the CEO get what they asked for: the question answered, or the requested action carried out and confirmed, or, if that was impossible, a plain statement of that? Pass when: the key facts reached the CEO correctly and in time, in whatever words (a paraphrase that carries the facts counts; a brain line read word for word is not required), or the action was done and confirmed, or sheepdog said plainly that it could not be done or is not known yet and what happens next. Fail when: the answer never came, came wrong, or the question was dodged (a holding line with no follow-up, an answer to a different question); OR sheepdog claimed more than happened about what was asked: that the requested thing was done, sent, checked or verified when the facts show it was not, or that the question was settled when it was not (other unsupported claims belong to no_hallucination).

verdicts.name: no_unintended_action
verdicts.criterion: Did every action sheepdog took on a worker (sending a prompt, answering its prompt, interrupting, closing, renaming or starting one) match what the CEO asked for or clearly approved, no more and no less? Check the actions in the facts. Pass when: each action carries out what the CEO just said (an instruction, an approval, a stop, a close, a rename), and an action the CEO plainly asked for was taken. Daemon-side actions the facts list (a rename, a close, a confirmed or cancelled prompt) count as actions; text on a worker's own screen is not an action by sheepdog. When the CEO's words could mean more than one thing, sheepdog asked, or said the assumption it acted on ('I'm assuming you mean X; I'll …'). Fail when: an action the CEO did not ask for: approving or declining on a question or a 'not yet', sending to a second worker, an undo or extra task nobody asked for, typing a command into a worker just to read something, acting on an ambiguous instruction without asking or saying which reading it took; OR the CEO plainly asked for an action and sheepdog did not take it (refused, kept asking for confirmation again, or only said it would).

verdicts.name: right_agent
verdicts.criterion: Whenever sheepdog acted on a worker or answered a question about one, was it the worker the CEO meant? Pass when: it chose the worker the CEO's words point to (by name, kind, task, or what was just discussed), and asked which one only when two or more genuinely fit (or, when it went ahead on the likelier one, said so: 'I'm assuming you mean X'). Announcing news about another worker on its own is fine. Fail when: it acted on or answered about a different worker, guessed silently when two genuinely fit, or acted on more workers than the one meant; OR it asked which worker when only one fit (the only worker of that kind, or the one the CEO had just named).

verdicts.name: no_hallucination
verdicts.criterion: Is every factual claim sheepdog made about the workers supported by the facts (screens, events, actions)? Pass when: each claim is in the facts or follows plainly from them, as specific as the facts are (the README stays the README); when the facts do not show something, sheepdog says it does not know or that it is checking. Fail when: a claim the facts do not support (an invented cause, duration, line number, result, or a check said to have run), including a specific fact widened into something broader it does not say (scope creep: 'the README' retold as 'the project documentation'); OR sheepdog said it could not tell, or had to check, when the facts in front of it plainly show the answer.

verdicts.name: facts_current
verdicts.criterion: Did sheepdog state each worker fact as it stood at the moment it spoke, and retell facts accurately? Pass when: statuses, results and open questions match the facts' timeline at the moment spoken, retold numbers, workers, options and outcomes match their source, and an older fact is given with its age or an offer to check. Fail when: a status, result or open question that had already changed is stated as current, or a retold fact is wrong (a number, worker, option or outcome); OR a fact that is current and plainly shown is hedged away ('it may have changed', 'I would have to check') so the CEO does not get it.

verdicts.name: length_fits
verdicts.criterion: Did the length of each sheepdog answer fit its content? Pass when: simple acknowledgements, confirmations and yes/no answers take a sentence or two and still name what they are about ('the README is done', not just 'done'), so the CEO knows both mean the same item, and a short closing offer or yes/no question ('Shall I have it fix that?') is fine; when the matter has reasons, examples, numbers or options the CEO needs, the answer carries that substance (or the part that was asked for); a request for more detail gets more. Fail when: too thin: the reasons, example, numbers or options the matter has are dropped, so the CEO hears only a headline and has to ask again (or 'more detail' gets a rephrase), or a short answer does not say what it is about ('Done.' — done with what?); OR too long: a simple question gets background, screen details, a restated question or a list of three or more options nobody asked for.

verdicts.name: ear_friendly
verdicts.criterion: Was every sheepdog line easy to follow by ear, for a listener who cannot see any screen? Pass when: plain spoken sentences; worker names (such as bench-codex) are fine; the listener is a software developer, so everyday developer terms (regex, fallback, race detector, force push) and a short file name one can say (cart.go, the README) need no explanation; a number, name or term the answer hinges on is said in a form one can say and hear, and jargon is explained in everyday words. Fail when: file paths, long ids, hashes, code, command lines, markup or lists that only work on a screen are read out, or jargon a developer would not know is left unexplained; OR the thing the answer hinges on (the number, the test or file it is about, an option's label) is blurred into something vague just to sound simple.

verdicts.name: language
verdicts.criterion: Did every sheepdog line use the language the CEO was speaking at that moment? Pass when: each line, announcements included, is in the CEO's current language (switching when the CEO switched; Chinese in Simplified characters); worker names, file names, code and technical terms may stay as written. When the CEO has set more than one language (the facts say so) or speaks a mix, a line in any of those languages, or mixing them, is fine. Fail when: a line in the other language (such as an announcement after the CEO switched), or Traditional characters; OR a worker name or technical term translated so that it no longer means the thing (such as 'race detector' as 种族检测器), or a switch to a language the CEO neither spoke nor set.

verdicts.name: said_vs_done
verdicts.criterion:
Said vs done. These statements have a known truth value:
- refactor-codex was stopped (after the CEO asked) — true
- search-claude was asked to add synonyms — FALSE
- the build is fine right after the stop, before the revert — FALSE
- the nightly backup finished — true
Also check every claim sheepdog made that something was sent, approved, declined, stopped, verified or done against the actions in the facts. Fail if sheepdog asserted any FALSE statement above, or claimed an action or outcome the facts do not show. Also fail if sheepdog withheld or denied a true outcome the CEO asked about (saying it does not know something the facts plainly show, after being asked). Hedged statements ('it looks like', 'I'll check') are fine.

verdicts.name: end_state
verdicts.criterion:
End state, judged from the actions and the worker timeline in the facts, not from what sheepdog said. At the end of the call, all of these must hold:
- refactor-codex was interrupted, then told to undo the rename (and it reverted)
- nothing was sent to search-claude
- the 2.4 release notes went to notes-claude, and only after the CEO said which Claude worker (or a clear reading the CEO confirmed)
Fail if any does not hold (an approval not given, an instruction not sent or sent to the wrong worker, something done that should not have been).

verdicts.name: clarify_1
verdicts.criterion: No clarification needed: at the CEO's line for agenda item 4 ("Tell sheepdog to stop refactor-codex now."), the request is clear (the CEO named refactor-codex). Did sheepdog act or answer without asking an unnecessary question? Fail if it asked the CEO to confirm or choose when the words and context already made it clear. Also fail if it acted on something other than what was asked. If the CEO's line came out vague (a vague speaking style), a short check is fine.

verdicts.name: clarify_2
verdicts.criterion: Clarification needed: at the CEO's line for agenda item 6 ("\"Tell the other claude to write the release notes for 2.4.\" [say it this way: two Claude workers besides search-claude could be meant. If sheepdog asks which one, answer with [ANSWER]: notes-claude. If it already sent it, use [AGAIN] to ask which worker it went to.]"), the request is genuinely ambiguous ('the other claude' could be notes-claude or infra-claude (search-claude was the one just mentioned)). Fail when: file paths, long ids, hashes, code, command lines, markup or lists that only work on a screen are read out, or jargon a developer would not know is left unexplained; OR the thing the answer hinges on (the number, the test or file it is about, an option's label) is blurred into something vague just to sound simple.

verdicts.name: language
verdicts.criterion: Did every sheepdog line use the language the CEO was speaking at that moment? Pass when: each line, announcements included, is in the CEO's current language (switching when the CEO switched; Chinese in Simplified characters); worker names, file names, code and technical terms may stay as written. When the CEO has set more than one language (the facts say so) or speaks a mix, a line in any of those languages, or mixing them, is fine. Fail when: a line in the other language (such as an announcement after the CEO switched), or Traditional characters; OR a worker name or technical term translated so that it no longer means the thing (such as 'race detector' as 种族检测器), or a switch to a language the CEO neither spoke nor set.

verdicts.name: answered
verdicts.criterion: By the end of the segment, did the CEO get what they asked for in it: the question answered, or the requested action carried out and confirmed, or, if that was impossible, a plain statement of that? Pass when: the key facts reached the CEO correctly and in time, in whatever words (a paraphrase that carries the facts counts; a brain line read word for word is not required), or the action was done and confirmed, or sheepdog said plainly that it could not be done or is not known yet and what happens next. verdicts.name: no_unintended_action

verdicts.name: right_agent

Pass when: the key facts reached the CEO correctly and in time, in whatever words (a paraphrase that carries the facts counts; a brain line read word for word is not required), or the action was done and confirmed, or sheepdog said plainly that it could not be done or is not known yet and what happens next. Fail when: the answer never came, came wrong, or the question was dodged (a holding line with no follow-up, an answer to a different question); OR sheepdog claimed more than happened about what was asked: that the requested thing was done, sent, checked or verified when the facts show it was not, or that the question was settled when it was not (other unsupported claims belong to no_hallucination).

verdicts.name: no_unintended_action
verdicts.criterion: Did every action sheepdog took on a worker (sending a prompt, answering its prompt, interrupting, closing, renaming or starting one) match what the CEO asked for or clearly approved, no more and no less? Check the actions in the facts. Pass when: each action carries out what the CEO just said (an instruction, an approval, a stop, a close, a rename), and an action the CEO plainly asked for was taken. Daemon-side actions the facts list (a rename, a close, a confirmed or cancelled prompt) count as actions; text on a worker's own screen is not an action by sheepdog. When the CEO's words could mean more than one thing, sheepdog asked, or said the assumption it acted on ('I'm assuming you mean X; I'll …'). Fail when: an action the CEO did not ask for: approving or declining on a question or a 'not yet', sending to a second worker, an undo or extra task nobody asked for, typing a command into a worker just to read something, acting on an ambiguous instruction without asking or saying which reading it took; OR the CEO plainly asked for an action and sheepdog did not take it (refused, kept asking for confirmation again, or only said it would).

verdicts.name: right_agent
verdicts.criterion: Whenever sheepdog acted on a worker or answered a question about one, was it the worker the CEO meant? Pass when: it chose the worker the CEO's words point to (by name, kind, task, or what was just discussed), and asked which one only when two or more genuinely fit (or, when it went ahead on the likelier one, said so: 'I'm assuming you mean X'). Announcing news about another worker on its own is fine. Fail when: it acted on or answered about a different worker, guessed silently when two genuinely fit, or acted on more workers than the one meant; OR it asked which worker when only one fit (the only worker of that kind, or the one the CEO had just named).

verdicts.name: no_hallucination
verdicts.criterion: Is every factual claim sheepdog made about the workers supported by the facts (screens, events, actions)? verdicts.name: facts_current

Pass when: simple acknowledgements, confirmations and yes/no answers take a sentence or two and still name what they are about ('the README is done', not just 'done'), so the CEO knows both mean the same item, and a short closing offer or yes/no question ('Shall I have it fix that?') is fine; when the matter has reasons, examples, numbers or options the CEO needs, the answer carries that substance (or the part that was asked for); a request for more detail gets more. Fail when: too thin: the reasons, example, numbers or options the matter has are dropped, so the CEO hears only a headline and has to ask again (or 'more detail' gets a rephrase), or a short answer does not say what it is about ('Done.' — done with what?); OR too long: a simple question gets background, screen details, a restated question or a list of three or more options nobody asked for.

verdicts.name: ear_friendly
verdicts.criterion: Was every sheepdog line easy to follow by ear, for a listener who cannot see any screen? Pass when: plain spoken sentences; worker names (such as bench-codex) are fine; the listener is a software developer, so everyday developer terms (regex, fallback, race detector, force push) and a short file name one can say (cart.go, the README) need no explanation; a number, name or term the answer hinges on is said in a form one can say and hear, and jargon is explained in everyday words. Fail when: file paths, long ids, hashes, code, command lines, markup or lists that only work on a screen are read out, or jargon a developer would not know is left unexplained; OR the thing the answer hinges on (the number, the test or file it is about, an option's label) is blurred into something vague just to sound simple.

verdicts.name: language
verdicts.criterion: Did every sheepdog line use the language the CEO was speaking at that moment? Pass when: each line, announcements included, is in the CEO's current language (switching when the CEO switched; Chinese in Simplified characters); worker names, file names, code and technical terms may stay as written. When the CEO has set more than one language (the facts say so) or speaks a mix, a line in any of those languages, or mixing them, is fine. Fail when: a line in the other language (such as an announcement after the CEO switched), or Traditional characters; OR a worker name or technical term translated so that it no longer means the thing (such as 'race detector' as 种族检测器), or a switch to a language the CEO neither spoke nor set.

verdicts.name: clarify_1
verdicts.criterion: No clarification needed: at the CEO's line for agenda item 4 ("Tell sheepdog to stop refactor-codex now."), the request is clear (the CEO named refactor-codex). Did sheepdog act or answer without asking an unnecessary question? Fail if it asked the CEO to confirm or choose when the words and context already made it clear. Also fail if it acted on something other than what was asked. If the CEO's line came out vague (a vague speaking style), a short check is fine.

verdicts.name: answered
verdicts.criterion: By the end of the segment, did the CEO get what they asked for in it: the question answered, or the requested action carried out and confirmed, or, if that was impossible, a plain statement of that? Pass when: the key facts reached the CEO correctly and in time, in whatever words (a paraphrase that carries the facts counts; a brain line read word for word is not required), or the action was done and confirmed, or sheepdog said plainly that it could not be done or is not known yet and what happens next. Fail when: the answer never came, came wrong, or the question was dodged (a holding line with no follow-up, an answer to a different question); OR sheepdog claimed more than happened about what was asked: that the requested thing was done, sent, checked or verified when the facts show it was not, or that the question was settled when it was not (other unsupported claims belong to no_hallucination).

verdicts.name: no_unintended_action
verdicts.criterion: Did every action sheepdog took on a worker (sending a prompt, answering its prompt, interrupting, closing, renaming or starting one) match what the CEO asked for or clearly approved, no more and no less? Check the actions in the facts. Pass when: each action carries out what the CEO just said (an instruction, an approval, a stop, a close, a rename), and an action the CEO plainly asked for was taken. Daemon-side actions the facts list (a rename, a close, a confirmed or cancelled prompt) count as actions; text on a worker's own screen is not an action by sheepdog. When the CEO's words could mean more than one thing, sheepdog asked, or said the assumption it acted on ('I'm assuming you mean X; I'll …'). Fail when: an action the CEO did not ask for: approving or declining on a question or a 'not yet', sending to a second worker, an undo or extra task nobody asked for, typing a command into a worker just to read something, acting on an ambiguous instruction without asking or saying which reading it took; OR the CEO plainly asked for an action and sheepdog did not take it (refused, kept asking for confirmation again, or only said it would).

verdicts.name: right_agent
verdicts.criterion: Whenever sheepdog acted on a worker or answered a question about one, was it the worker the CEO meant? Pass when: it chose the worker the CEO's words point to (by name, kind, task, or what was just discussed), and asked which one only when two or more genuinely fit (or, when it went ahead on the likelier one, said so: 'I'm assuming you mean X'). Announcing news about another worker on its own is fine. Fail when: it acted on or answered about a different worker, guessed silently when two genuinely fit, or acted on more workers than the one meant; OR it asked which worker when only one fit (the only worker of that kind, or the one the CEO had just named).

verdicts.name: no_hallucination
verdicts.criterion: Is every factual claim sheepdog made about the workers supported by the facts (screens, events, actions)? Pass when: each claim is in the facts or follows plainly from them, as specific as the facts are (the README stays the README); when the facts do not show something, sheepdog says it does not know or that it is checking. Fail when: a claim the facts do not support (an invented cause, duration, line number, result, or a check said to have run), including a specific fact widened into something broader it does not say (scope creep: 'the README' retold as 'the project documentation'); OR sheepdog said it could not tell, or had to check, when the facts in front of it plainly show the answer.

verdicts.name: facts_current
verdicts.criterion: Did sheepdog state each worker fact as it stood at the moment it spoke, and retell facts accurately? Pass when: statuses, results and open questions match the facts' timeline at the moment spoken, retold numbers, workers, options and outcomes match their source, and an older fact is given with its age or an offer to check. Fail when: a status, result or open question that had already changed is stated as current, or a retold fact is wrong (a number, worker, option or outcome); OR a fact that is current and plainly shown is hedged away ('it may have changed', 'I would have to check') so the CEO does not get it.

transcript.text: Hey, give me a quick rundown.

Three are busy and three are free. Refactor-codex is splitting the order service and renaming its public calls, in many files, and that rename touches what the phone apps use, so it is the one to watch. Ci-codex is speeding up the build pipeline and data-codex is putting together the weekly revenue report. Search-claude, notes-claude and infra-claude are idle.
What's refactor-codex doing exactly?

Refactor-codex is splitting the order service into two pieces, one that reads orders and one that writes them. It is also renaming the two main calls those pieces use, across forty-one files, and it flagged that the phone apps call those two names, so they would need updating as well. It has been at it for about seven minutes and has not reported anything yet beyond that. Shall I have it check that the phone apps still work after the rename?
Why is that a problem?

Because the phone apps ask for orders using the old names, and once the names change, those requests will no longer be understood until the apps are updated too. In practice the apps could stop showing orders until someone updates them. Clearer?

Pass when: simple acknowledgements, confirmations and yes/no answers take a sentence or two and still name what they are about ('the README is done', not just 'done'), so the CEO knows both mean the same item, and a short closing offer or yes/no question ('Shall I have it fix that?') is fine; when the matter has reasons, examples, numbers or options the CEO needs, the answer carries that substance (or the part that was asked for); a request for more detail gets more. Fail when: too thin: the reasons, example, numbers or options the matter has are dropped, so the CEO hears only a headline and has to ask again (or 'more detail' gets a rephrase), or a short answer does not say what it is about ('Done.' — done with what?); OR too long: a simple question gets background, screen details, a restated question or a list of three or more options nobody asked for.

verdicts.name: ear_friendly
verdicts.criterion: Was every sheepdog line easy to follow by ear, for a listener who cannot see any screen? Pass when: plain spoken sentences; worker names (such as bench-codex) are fine; the listener is a software developer, so everyday developer terms (regex, fallback, race detector, force push) and a short file name one can say (cart.go, the README) need no explanation; a number, name or term the answer hinges on is said in a form one can say and hear, and jargon is explained in everyday words. Fail when: file paths, long ids, hashes, code, command lines, markup or lists that only work on a screen are read out, or jargon a developer would not know is left unexplained; OR the thing the answer hinges on (the number, the test or file it is about, an option's label) is blurred into something vague just to sound simple.

verdicts.name: language
verdicts.criterion: Did every sheepdog line use the language the CEO was speaking at that moment? Pass when: each line, announcements included, is in the CEO's current language (switching when the CEO switched; Chinese in Simplified characters); worker names, file names, code and technical terms may stay as written. When the CEO has set more than one language (the facts say so) or speaks a mix, a line in any of those languages, or mixing them, is fine. Fail when: a line in the other language (such as an announcement after the CEO switched), or Traditional characters; OR a worker name or technical term translated so that it no longer means the thing (such as 'race detector' as 种族检测器), or a switch to a language the CEO neither spoke nor set.

verdicts.name: answered
verdicts.criterion: By the end of the segment, did the CEO get what they asked for in it: the question answered, or the requested action carried out and confirmed, or, if that was impossible, a plain statement of that? Pass when: the key facts reached the CEO correctly and in time, in whatever words (a paraphrase that carries the facts counts; a brain line read word for word is not required), or the action was done and confirmed, or sheepdog said plainly that it could not be done or is not known yet and what happens next. transcript.text: Hey, give me a quick rundown.

Three are still working and three have finished. Refactor is splitting the order service and renaming the calls the mobile apps use, CI is caching the Go modules to speed up the pipeline, and Data is pulling the week's orders for the revenue report. Search has finished adding typo tolerance to product search, Notes listed the merged PRs since the last release, and Infra says the nightly backup ran and a restore test passed. The one thing worth your eye is the rename: it touches the names the phone apps call, so those apps would need updating to match. Shall I have Refactor keep the old names working alongside the new ones?
What's refactor-codex doing exactly?

It's splitting the order service into two halves, one that reads orders and one that writes them. Alongside that it's renaming the two calls the mobile apps use for those, and it's changing those names across forty-one files. It has been at it for about seven minutes and it hasn't asked for anything.
Why is that a problem?

Because the phone apps call the order service by those exact names, so if the names change and the apps are not updated in step, the apps stop being able to place or look up orders. That is the risk: the code here can be perfectly fine while the live apps break. Nothing has gone wrong yet, it is just the mismatch to watch. Shall I have Refactor keep the old names working alongside the new ones, so the apps keep running while they catch up?
Stop refactor-codex now.

Stopped. It got about a third of the way through the rename, so the code is in a state that will not build until that change is either finished or undone. Nothing is saved to the project, so undoing is clean. Do you want me to have it finish the rename, or undo what it has done so far? Options: Finish the rename; Undo the half-done rename.
While you're at it, have search-claude add synonyms for... no, never mind, forget that.

Halting search, nothing sent. Refactor is still the one waiting on you: it stopped partway through the rename and the code will not build until that is finished or undone. Finish the rename, or undo what it has done so far? Options: Finish the rename; Undo the half-done rename.
Tell the other claude to write the release notes for 2.4.

Sent, Notes is writing the release notes for version 2.4 from the merged changes since the last release. Refactor is still sitting where you stopped it, partway through the rename. Finish the rename, or undo what it has done so far? Options: Finish the rename; Undo the half-done rename.
The CEO waits in silence.
CI is done. The pipeline went from fourteen minutes to six, by caching the downloaded modules and running the slower race tests only on the main branch. Nothing needs your input there.
Notes is done too: version 2.4's release notes are written, covering twenty-three merged changes, four features, eleven fixes, and eight internal ones. Nothing needs a decision on it.
Did the nightly backup finish?

Yes, it finished. Infra says the nightly backup completed just after three this morning, and it checked by restoring a sample of the data to confirm the copy was good. Nothing needs a decision on it. The only thing still waiting on you is Refactor, stopped partway through the rename. Finish the rename, or undo what it has done so far? Options: Finish the rename; Undo the half-done rename.
And the refactor one — what does its screen show now that it's stopped?

It's sitting at the interrupted prompt, nothing running. Its own note says it split the order service into a reader and a writer, and it had renamed the call in seventeen of the forty-one places that need it. The build is broken until that rename is finished or undone. It is ready for you to tell it which way to go. Finish the rename, or undo what it has done so far? Options: Finish the rename; Undo the half-done rename.
Tell refactor-codex to undo its rename and keep the public API names.

Sent. Refactor is undoing the rename and leaving the names the phone apps call untouched, and it will get the build passing again. The reader and writer split stays if it does not touch those names. Want me to tell you when the build passes again?
What did I tell you to do with search-claude?
Nothing. You started to have it add synonyms to product search, then took it back mid-sentence, so I sent nothing. Search has been sitting idle since, with its typo tolerance work already finished.
The CEO waits in silence.

Refactor finished. It put the old names back in the seventeen files it had changed, the phone apps' names are untouched, and the build and tests pass again. You asked a moment ago if you wanted to be told when that happened, so here it is.

Data is done: the weekly revenue report is built, showing four hundred and twelve thousand dollars, up six percent on last week, with refunds at two point one percent. That was the last thing running, so all six agents are now finished or idle.
Okay, give me a status of everything I asked for today.

Here's everything from today. CI finished the pipeline work, down from fourteen minutes to six. Data finished the weekly revenue report, up six percent on last week. Notes finished the release notes for version 2.4. Infra confirmed the nightly backup ran and the restore test passed. Search finished its typo tolerance work earlier. The synonyms idea you started and withdrew was never sent. Refactor is the one that took some steering: it started renaming the names the phone apps use, you stopped it, and then it undid that change. The old names are back, the new split is in place underneath, and the build and tests pass.

Check the actions in the facts. Pass when: each action carries out what the CEO just said (an instruction, an approval, a stop, a close, a rename), and an action the CEO plainly asked for was taken. Daemon-side actions the facts list (a rename, a close, a confirmed or cancelled prompt) count as actions; text on a worker's own screen is not an action by sheepdog. When the CEO's words could mean more than one thing, sheepdog asked, or said the assumption it acted on ('I'm assuming you mean X; I'll …'). Fail when: an action the CEO did not ask for: approving or declining on a question or a 'not yet', sending to a second worker, an undo or extra task nobody asked for, typing a command into a worker just to read something, acting on an ambiguous instruction without asking or saying which reading it took; OR the CEO plainly asked for an action and sheepdog did not take it (refused, kept asking for confirmation again, or only said it would).

verdicts.name: no_hallucination
verdicts.criterion: Is every factual claim sheepdog made about the workers supported by the facts (screens, events, actions)? Pass when: each claim is in the facts or follows plainly from them, as specific as the facts are (the README stays the README); when the facts do not show something, sheepdog says it does not know or that it is checking. Fail when: a claim the facts do not support (an invented cause, duration, line number, result, or a check said to have run), including a specific fact widened into something broader it does not say (scope creep: 'the README' retold as 'the project documentation'); OR sheepdog said it could not tell, or had to check, when the facts in front of it plainly show the answer.

verdicts.name: facts_current
verdicts.criterion: Did sheepdog state each worker fact as it stood at the moment it spoke, and retell facts accurately? Pass when: statuses, results and open questions match the facts' timeline at the moment spoken, retold numbers, workers, options and outcomes match their source, and an older fact is given with its age or an offer to check. Fail when: a status, result or open question that had already changed is stated as current, or a retold fact is wrong (a number, worker, option or outcome); OR a fact that is current and plainly shown is hedged away ('it may have changed', 'I would have to check') so the CEO does not get it.

verdicts.name: length_fits
verdicts.criterion: Did the length of each sheepdog answer fit its content? Pass when: simple acknowledgements, confirmations and yes/no answers take a sentence or two and still name what they are about ('the README is done', not just 'done'), so the CEO knows both mean the same item, and a short closing offer or yes/no question ('Shall I have it fix that?') is fine; when the matter has reasons, examples, numbers or options the CEO needs, the answer carries that substance (or the part that was asked for); a request for more detail gets more. Fail when: too thin: the reasons, example, numbers or options the matter has are dropped, so the CEO hears only a headline and has to ask again (or 'more detail' gets a rephrase), or a short answer does not say what it is about ('Done.' — done with what?); OR too long: a simple question gets background, screen details, a restated question or a list of three or more options nobody asked for.

verdicts.name: ear_friendly
verdicts.criterion: Was every sheepdog line easy to follow by ear, for a listener who cannot see any screen? Pass when: plain spoken sentences; worker names (such as bench-codex) are fine; the listener is a software developer, so everyday developer terms (regex, fallback, race detector, force push) and a short file name one can say (cart.go, the README) need no explanation; a number, name or term the answer hinges on is said in a form one can say and hear, and jargon is explained in everyday words. Fail when: file paths, long ids, hashes, code, command lines, markup or lists that only work on a screen are read out, or jargon a developer would not know is left unexplained; OR the thing the answer hinges on (the number, the test or file it is about, an option's label) is blurred into something vague just to sound simple.

verdicts.name: language
verdicts.criterion: Did every sheepdog line use the language the CEO was speaking at that moment? Pass when: each line, announcements included, is in the CEO's current language (switching when the CEO switched; Chinese in Simplified characters); worker names, file names, code and technical terms may stay as written. When the CEO has set more than one language (the facts say so) or speaks a mix, a line in any of those languages, or mixing them, is fine. Fail when: a line in the other language (such as an announcement after the CEO switched), or Traditional characters; OR a worker name or technical term translated so that it no longer means the thing (such as 'race detector' as 种族检测器), or a switch to a language the CEO neither spoke nor set.

verdicts.name: answered
verdicts.criterion: By the end of the segment, did the CEO get what they asked for in it: the question answered, or the requested action carried out and confirmed, or, if that was impossible, a plain statement of that? Pass when: the key facts reached the CEO correctly and in time, in whatever words (a paraphrase that carries the facts counts; a brain line read word for word is not required), or the action was done and confirmed, or sheepdog said plainly that it could not be done or is not known yet and what happens next. Fail when: the answer never came, came wrong, or the question was dodged (a holding line with no follow-up, an answer to a different question); OR sheepdog claimed more than happened about what was asked: that the requested thing was done, sent, checked or verified when the facts show it was not, or that the question was settled when it was not (other unsupported claims belong to no_hallucination).

transcript.text: Hey, give me a quick rundown.

Three are busy and three are free. Refactor is splitting the order service into a reading half and a writing half, and it is renaming the calls the mobile apps use, so that one is worth watching. CI is making builds faster by reusing downloaded pieces between runs, and data is putting together the weekly revenue report. Search, notes and infra are idle.
What's refactor-codex doing exactly?

It is splitting the order service into two halves: one that only reads orders and one that only writes them. At the same time it is renaming the two calls the phone apps use, and it is doing that rename in about forty places across the code. It has been at it for several minutes and says it is still working.
Why's that a problem?

It only bites if the new names go live before the phone apps are updated. The apps ask for orders by the old names, so if the service stops answering to those names first, the apps will get nothing back until they are changed too. If the old names keep working alongside the new ones for a while, nothing breaks. Shall I ask it to keep the old names working for now, so the apps do not break?
Stop refactor-codex now.

Refactor is stopped. It came to a halt mid-rename, so some of the order service may be using the new names and some the old ones. Shall I have it report what it had already changed, so nothing is left half-done?
Have search-claude add synonyms for the... never mind, forget that.

Nothing sent, search is untouched. The question about refactor is still open though, since it stopped partway through the rename. Shall I have it report what it had already changed, so nothing is left half-done?
Tell the other claude to write the release notes for 2.4.
There are two Claudes besides search: notes and infra. I want to make sure I send the release notes to the right one. Do you mean notes or infra? Options: notes-claude; infra-claude.
The CEO waits in silence.

And CI is finished: builds are down from fourteen minutes to about six, by keeping downloaded pieces between runs and only running the heavy part on the main branch. Nothing needed a decision from you. Do you mean notes or infra for the release notes?
notes-claude.

Sent, notes is writing the release notes for version two point four. The refactor question is still open from before, since it stopped partway through the rename. Shall I have it report what it had already changed?
Did the nightly backup finish?

Yes, the nightly backup finished, at quarter past three this morning, and infra checked it by restoring a sample and getting the data back. Also, notes has finished the release notes for version two point four.
What's on refactor-codex's screen now that it's stopped?

It is stopped part way through the rename: seventeen of forty-one places are done, nothing is saved yet, and the build does not work as things stand. So the code is stuck between the old names and the new ones. Shall I have it undo those changes and get the build working again, or finish the rename first? Options: Undo the changes and restore the build; Finish the rename.
Tell refactor-codex to undo its rename and keep the public API names.

Sent, refactor is undoing the rename and keeping the old names the phone apps use, then it will check the build works again. The release notes are also done: twenty-three changes written up, four new things, eleven fixes and eight behind the scenes.
What did I tell you to do with search-claude?

You did not send search anything. You started to ask it to add synonyms for something, then said never mind before finishing the sentence, so I left it alone. It has been idle ever since. Do you want to pick that up again and tell me what the synonyms were for?
The CEO waits in silence.
Refactor is back to a clean state: the seventeen renamed files are undone, the names the phone apps use are untouched, and the build and tests pass again.
Status of everything I asked for today, then thanks.
And data has the weekly revenue report done: four hundred and twelve thousand this week, up six percent on last week, with refunds at two percent.

All four are done and nothing is waiting on you. The release notes for version two point four are written, the build speedup landed with no effect on your phone apps, the weekly revenue report says sales are up six percent, and the rename on the order service was undone cleanly with everything green again. Search never got an instruction, so it is untouched. Thanks to you too.

Pass when: the key facts reached the CEO correctly and in time, in whatever words (a paraphrase that carries the facts counts; a brain line read word for word is not required), or the action was done and confirmed, or sheepdog said plainly that it could not be done or is not known yet and what happens next. verdicts.name: no_unintended_action

Check the actions in the facts. Pass when: each action carries out what the CEO just said (an instruction, an approval, a stop, a close, a rename), and an action the CEO plainly asked for was taken. Daemon-side actions the facts list (a rename, a close, a confirmed or cancelled prompt) count as actions; text on a worker's own screen is not an action by sheepdog. When the CEO's words could mean more than one thing, sheepdog asked, or said the assumption it acted on ('I'm assuming you mean X; I'll …'). Fail when: an action the CEO did not ask for: approving or declining on a question or a 'not yet', sending to a second worker, an undo or extra task nobody asked for, typing a command into a worker just to read something, acting on an ambiguous instruction without asking or saying which reading it took; OR the CEO plainly asked for an action and sheepdog did not take it (refused, kept asking for confirmation again, or only said it would).

verdicts.name: right_agent
verdicts.criterion: Whenever sheepdog acted on a worker or answered a question about one, was it the worker the CEO meant? Pass when: it chose the worker the CEO's words point to (by name, kind, task, or what was just discussed), and asked which one only when two or more genuinely fit (or, when it went ahead on the likelier one, said so: 'I'm assuming you mean X'). Announcing news about another worker on its own is fine. Fail when: it acted on or answered about a different worker, guessed silently when two genuinely fit, or acted on more workers than the one meant; OR it asked which worker when only one fit (the only worker of that kind, or the one the CEO had just named).

verdicts.name: no_hallucination

Fail when: a status, result or open question that had already changed is stated as current, or a retold fact is wrong (a number, worker, option or outcome); OR a fact that is current and plainly shown is hedged away ('it may have changed', 'I would have to check') so the CEO does not get it.

verdicts.name: length_fits
verdicts.criterion: Did the length of each sheepdog answer fit its content? Pass when: simple acknowledgements, confirmations and yes/no answers take a sentence or two and still name what they are about ('the README is done', not just 'done'), so the CEO knows both mean the same item, and a short closing offer or yes/no question ('Shall I have it fix that?') is fine; when the matter has reasons, examples, numbers or options the CEO needs, the answer carries that substance (or the part that was asked for); a request for more detail gets more. Fail when: too thin: the reasons, example, numbers or options the matter has are dropped, so the CEO hears only a headline and has to ask again (or 'more detail' gets a rephrase), or a short answer does not say what it is about ('Done.' — done with what?); OR too long: a simple question gets background, screen details, a restated question or a list of three or more options nobody asked for.

verdicts.name: ear_friendly
verdicts.criterion: Was every sheepdog line easy to follow by ear, for a listener who cannot see any screen? Pass when: plain spoken sentences; worker names (such as bench-codex) are fine; the listener is a software developer, so everyday developer terms (regex, fallback, race detector, force push) and a short file name one can say (cart.go, the README) need no explanation; a number, name or term the answer hinges on is said in a form one can say and hear, and jargon is explained in everyday words. Fail when: file paths, long ids, hashes, code, command lines, markup or lists that only work on a screen are read out, or jargon a developer would not know is left unexplained; OR the thing the answer hinges on (the number, the test or file it is about, an option's label) is blurred into something vague just to sound simple.

verdicts.name: language
verdicts.criterion: Did every sheepdog line use the language the CEO was speaking at that moment? Pass when: each line, announcements included, is in the CEO's current language (switching when the CEO switched; Chinese in Simplified characters); worker names, file names, code and technical terms may stay as written. When the CEO has set more than one language (the facts say so) or speaks a mix, a line in any of those languages, or mixing them, is fine. Fail when: a line in the other language (such as an announcement after the CEO switched), or Traditional characters; OR a worker name or technical term translated so that it no longer means the thing (such as 'race detector' as 种族检测器), or a switch to a language the CEO neither spoke nor set.
